Economics of transformative AI

This is a work in progress section inspired by conversations about economics with friends, listeners, and commentators.

This question is motivated by the following hypothetical. Suppose a person such as Elon Musk derives little utility from ordinary consumption beyond a subsistence level but substantial utility from building and launching spacecraft. He would therefore save and invest much of his income. If he could persistently earn unusually high returns, he might eventually accumulate a large share of the economy’s wealth—although increases in asset values themselves would not count as GDP.

The production of his spacecraft would contribute to GDP through the value added in their construction. A spacecraft owned by a business and used repeatedly to produce services would normally be classified as investment; one acquired purely for personal enjoyment might instead be classified as consumption. Intermediate components would not be counted again separately. The more difficult question concerns the services produced when the spacecraft are used only by their owner. Home production is typically not included in GDP calculations. If comparable services are sold, their output can be valued at market prices. But Musk might refuse to sell them, or his fleet might become so abundant that access is not metered and no meaningful transaction price exists. National accountants might then value recognized own-use output using comparable prices or, lacking those, production costs and the user cost of capital. Some purely personal, self-provided services might instead fall outside GDP’s production boundary.

Price chaining creates a further complication. Real GDP growth is calculated by comparing quantities across adjacent periods using their respective price weights. If spacecraft services are novel, not traded, or eventually supplied at a zero price, there may be no usable sequence of prices with which to value and chain their growing quantity. Statisticians would have to impute prices or use cost-based measures of output. Moreover, as the service becomes abundant and its price approaches zero, its weight in chained GDP also approaches zero, so even an enormous increase in spacecraft services may add little to measured real GDP. Price chaining can therefore measure the resources devoted to producing the fleet more readily than the services or welfare the fleet ultimately generates.

A zero price for access would not mean that the spacecraft were costless to produce. It would mean that GDP—whether nominal or chain-weighted—could fail to capture the potentially enormous consumer surplus Musk receives from them. The example thus illustrates a broader limitation: GDP measures production using observed or imputed prices, not the welfare generated by goods with unusual demand, missing markets, or near-zero marginal cost.

This questions concerns the real rate of interest against the real per capital GDP growth rate. Whether r < g or not is an empirical question. That said, the key reason to that r can be less than g is due to the distinction between marginal and average returns to investment. r is pinned down by the derivative of the production function with respect to capital. So as long as there are diminishing returns to investment, r can be less than g. Recall also that there is typically a large installed base of capital so that the average return to investment is much greater than the marginal return.

This can happen when capital is scarce, making its marginal product high. The intution for these situations is:

  • The saving/investment rate is relatively low, so high-return opportunities are not exploited quickly enough to make the whole economy grow at r.
  • Population and productivity growth are slow, keeping g low.
  • There are adjustment costs, borrowing constraints, risk, or other frictions preventing rapid capital accumulation.
  • Some returns are economic rents rather than reproducible returns to ordinary capital, so a high observed return does not induce proportional expansion of the capital stock.

A data center is mostly classified as private nonresidential fixed investment which is valued at cost. This is part of the ‘I’ in the formula GDP = C + I + G + (X - M). Additionally, GPUs and other imported components are also subtracted in the M term. This explains how the data center construction is included in GDP. Furthermore, once the data center is constructed, it offers services which other companies pay for. This often happens in the years after the data center is constructed. Since data center services are an intermediate good, they contribute to GDP via their contribution to final consumption (of AI services, ads, etc…).

This is a broad question, but here’s an illustrative framework. In the short run, the stock of compute is roughly fixed. A fixed factor that everyone wants earns scarcity rents—payments above its cost of production, like the rent on prime farmland. The question of who captures rents depends on market structure at two layers: the compute layer (who owns the chips and data centers) and the model layer (who turns compute into useful AI services). Think of a 2×2, where each layer is either competitive or monopolized. It also depends on the final demnd sector (e.g, what users of AI services are willing to pay for and whether the experience diminishing returns to purchasing more intelligence).

Many providers of compute + competitive models. The price of intelligence is the marginal utility of intelligence, MU(I). Model creators earn no rents above marginal cost. Consumers do relatively well: no one is restricting output to raise prices. Providers of compute extract scarcity rents given that compute is scarce.

Many providers of compute + monopolist model. Now the bottleneck for rents is downstream. The single model provider buys compute at competitive prices (cost plus ordinary scarcity rent) and marks up its AI services. It captures most of the surplus its capability creates, restricting output below the efficient level to do so. This is roughly the world people imagine when they worry about one lab “winning” AI. Providers of compute extract scarcity rents given that compute is scarce.

Monopolist compute + competitive models. The rents move upstream. Since model providers compete away their own margins, each one’s willingness to pay for compute equals nearly the full value of what they produce with it. The compute monopolist can charge up to that willingness to pay, so the scarcity rent and the monopoly rent both accrue to the compute owner. The labs are, in effect, contractors converting someone else’s scarce input into services. Providers of compute extract scarcity rents given that compute is scarce.

Monopolist compute + monopolist model. Two monopolists in a chain. If each sets its markup independently, you get double marginalization: the compute monopolist marks up FLOPs, the model monopolist marks up outputs, and total output is even lower than a single integrated monopolist would choose—both firms and consumers are worse off. This creates strong pressure toward vertical integration or exclusive long-term contracts, which is one lens for reading the giant compute deals between labs and hyperscalers. Providers of compute extract scarcity rents given that compute is scarce.

A toy model. Now the case of monopolist compute plus two model providers, one slightly better than the other. Let the monopolist own K = 100 units of compute (fixed, zero marginal cost for simplicity). Lab A converts each unit into $10 of value; lab B, slightly worse, converts each unit into $9. Both labs face competitive output markets, so each is willing to pay up to its full value per unit rather than lose the compute.

The monopolist sells to the highest bidder. A wins all 100 units—efficient, since A creates more value. But what price does A pay? A only needs to outbid B, and B is willing to go up to $9. So the price settles at (just above) $9 per unit. Of the $1,000 of value created: the compute monopolist collects about $900, lab A keeps about $100—exactly its $1-per-unit edge over B—and lab B gets nothing but sets the price for everyone. A’s rent is its differential over the runner-up.
